chapter: Minton's, Louis Armstrong and the South
title: Replaced by Neil Spencer; left behind in a Georgia town
summary: Manager Joe Glaser insisted on a bigger name, so Clarke was fired by the road manager and left on a dark street in Georgia with his drums as the band left.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: It was wonderful. And we were just getting to be a family, and Joe Glazer said, 'You've got to get Kenny Clarke out of there. He has no -- who knows Kenny Clarke?' So Pops said, 'Leave the kid alone. Leave the kid alone.
He'll be all right." Glazer said, "No, Pops. We've got to have a name there." You know, because after Big Sid, you know, and then here I come. I'm nobody, you know. So they hired old Neil Spencer.
That's a shame when a manager puts his two cents in, isn't it?
Oh, we were just getting to be really --
What a shame. Oh, Neil Spencer didn't have such a big name anyway.

No, but he had been with Kirby, John Kirby and all that, you know. His name was much -- no-one knew who I was. They said, "That little kid who drops the bombs." That was about the biggest name I ever got. "That little kid who drops the bombs up at Minton's. You remember what's his name?"
(Laughter)
So that was about the size of it.
So what happened then? How long did it last? Was it like nine months or something?

Well, let me see. We played -- this was before the war, now. We played Jacksonville Beach. Then we did Waycross, Georgia. We did a southern tour, you know, all that. And then they were on their way to Henderson, Texas when I was told that I wouldn't be leaving for Henderson with the band. So they left me in a little town in Georgia, alone.
Oh, now, that's disgusting.
With my drums.
Oh, they didn't.
And it was after the dance, which it was like a little town in Georgia, had no street lights. And there I was --
Why, that's a dangerous, awful thing to do.
And there I was in some town in Georgia. I don't know where.
And you were young, too.
Yeah, I was just a kid. And then, after the bus pulled out --
Well, how --
Well, it was on account of Joe Glazer and this road manager.
What a way of doing -- who was the road manager?
George Kroll his name was.
How disgusting. I know that Pops didn't ever stick his neck out on that kind of thing.
No, he wouldn't.
No.

And he wouldn't know until the dance was half over that I was leaving the band that night. That's why he cried. And he looked out of the bus and he said, 'Bye, Gizzard.' And the bus pulled out, and there I was,
standing with my drums, in some dark street, in some town in Georgia.
